items.title: I still don't understand why everyone is not using this yet. Thanks to it, a year ago I increased my income to 17,000 do
items.summary:
I still don't understand why everyone is not using this yet. Thanks to it, a year ago I increased my income to 17,000 dollars a month

Andrey Karpathy, co-founder of OpenAI, published a simple idea that got 16 million views: stop using AI to write code, use it to build a second brain

You point Claude Code to a folder, drop any source in there (an article, transcript, PDF) and Claude reads it, links it, and saves it into a living wiki of everything you know. It compounds like interest: the more you feed it, the smarter it gets

Here is the gist:

Install Obsidian, create a vault, open it in Claude Code

Paste the file with Karpathy's wiki idea and tell Claude to build it

Claude creates three folders: raw for sources, wiki for its pages, CLAUDE
which runs everything

Drop any source into raw and say "ingest this"

Ask questions across everything, forever

Five minutes to set up, and you never start with an empty chat again

The full step-by-step guide is in the article. Save to bookmarks

items.title: We built Pando, a new Git backend for our monorepo, to handle more pushes and fetches without changing how our engineers
items.summary:
We built Pando, a new Git backend for our monorepo, to handle more pushes and fetches without changing how our engineers and agents use Git.

Pando cut push latency by ~80% and now serves nearly a petabyte of Git data a day. We can grow Git capacity alongside agent usage. https://t.co/4c0YXOfKqK

items.title: Terence Tao says that the AI proof on the Navier–Stokes problem is correct, yet mathematicians learned almost nothing fr
items.summary:
Terence Tao says that the AI proof on the Navier–Stokes problem is correct, yet mathematicians learned almost nothing from it. The proof is 100 pages, AI-generated and full of issues in its text, but a formal certificate in the language Lean confirms it.

Navier–Stokes is a Millennium Prize problem that asks whether the equations for fluids like water can start smooth and then blow up, with velocity or pressure becoming infinite. Human mathematicians came very close, and OpenAI ran its biggest model, with millions of dollars of compute, to get there first.

A human proof normally comes with talks on what was tried, what worked and what it connects to, like picking fruit and planting the seeds. Tao calls this one strip mining: the fruit taken, the landscape left barren. One colleague, using lots of AI, could explain only half of it after days of work.

items.title: We built Control Room, a central system to track model workloads across our research infrastructure and stop them quickl
items.summary:
We built Control Room, a central system to track model workloads across our research infrastructure and stop them quickly when safety or security concerns arise.

It connects every research inference workload, including agentic sampling for model training and evaluation, data processing, and more. This works together with our misalignment monitoring systems, and halts model output within 35 seconds of a decision to intervene to stop or pause a job.

Control Room is just one part of our holistic approach for safe frontier model training and deployment.

https://t.co/tc0lBqFdS5

items.title: this is f*cking insane. andrej karpathy: "the biggest regret of every engineer in my field right now is every AI convers
items.summary:
this is f*cking insane. andrej karpathy: "the biggest regret of every engineer in my field right now is every AI conversation they never saved, and in 10 years the ones who started saving in 2024 will be running circles around the rest of us"

andrej karpathy, co-founder of openai, pulled 16M views on one idea: stop using AI to write code, use it to build a second brain that remembers every article, pdf, transcript and conversation you ever fed it

you point claude code at a folder, drop anything into it, and claude reads it, cross-links it with everything already there, and writes it into a living wiki. your knowledge finally compounds instead of leaking out of your head every friday

the stack:

→ brew install obsidian, mkdir ~/vault, cd ~/vault
→ run claude in that folder and type "init a knowledge vault with CLAUDE.md as the rules, /raw for sources, /wiki for your pages"
→ drop any file into /raw (youtube transcript, meeting notes, 400-page pdf, screenshot of a tweet) and type "ingest"
→ claude writes a wiki page, links it to 5 existing ones automatically, updates CLAUDE.md with any new pattern it noticed about how you think
→ never open a blank claude chat again. every question goes through the vault, every answer cites your own sources with dates and links

5 minutes to set up. compounding knowledge from that evening forward

the ugly part most will scroll past: in 10 years the engineers who started this in 2024 will remember every book, every podcast, every meeting with receipts. you will remember none of them. karpathy already picked which side he is on and you are still not on his

full step-by-step is in the article below

bookmark this before you waste another monday
